_comment: The text prompt each rig's motion was generated from, keyed by its file in resources/glbs/. Read by js/viewer.js and drawn as a chip pinned above the model in the interactive viewer; a stage in js/examples.js can override one with a per-file `prompt`. House style is the paper's own captioning format (Appendix A.5): 'An [object type] [action].' — one sentence, under 12 words, ONE dominant action, a direction only where it is clearly observed, no adverbs, and no appearance or scene words. Name the object concretely, as the demo videos do ('A robot', 'An eagle', 'A jellyfish'), not as 'An object'.
_sources: Two channels. (1) The lines listed in _from_caption are the ORIGINAL prompts, read off the captions burned into assets/: diverse-1..3.mp4 and prompt-eagle/-shark/-bighero.mp4 caption the same rigs this viewer loads. (2) Every other line was written from the motion itself — each glb was imported into Blender headless, sampled for travel / rise / yaw / per-limb activity, and rendered as a 6-frame filmstrip to look at, since every clip's animation is named 'Reconstructed_Action' and so says nothing about itself. Those describe what the rig actually does, but they are not the prompt the model was given; swap in the real ones where you have them.
_from_author: chicken.glb, stego-attack.glb ('attacks forward') and monster.glb ('walks in place') were corrected by the author. They are the warning against trusting a render: the peck-like head dip and the stego's rear-up both LOOK like precise verbs, but this dataset reuses a small vocabulary — 'attacks forward' is also the caption on the piranha plant. Match an existing caption before inventing a verb.
